standard.title: Continuities and Changes Around the Turn of the 20th Century
standard.description: continuities and changes and their effects on ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe causes and effects of change and identify continuities in earlier periods (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K08, AC9HH8K13). They have not yet examined living conditions and material culture in Australia around 1900, the specific legal reforms of the new Federal Parliament, or how to systematically apply the concepts of continuity and change across multiple domains simultaneously.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine living and working conditions in Australia around 1900, compare different settings, identify features of housing, sanitation, transport, education and industry, compare these with conditions around 1800, and explain how federal laws such as the Harvester Judgment affected living and working conditions.

nodes.label: Continuity and change as analytical tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the concepts of continuity and change as analytical lenses — that continuity and change always coexist, that what changes and what persists are both historically significant — and apply this framework to a simple example.
nodes.minimum_width: Students distinguish continuity (what persisted) from change (what transformed) and explain that both require explanation — it is not enough to describe change, continuities must also be explained and vice versa.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply continuity-and-change thinking to a familiar domain (e.g. transport or housing); explain that the rate and extent of change varies across different aspects of life (some things transform rapidly, others persist across generations); recognise that what counts as continuity or change depends on what time period and what aspects of life are being examined; understand that the same period can show rapid change in some domains and strong continuity in others.
wider: Apply the concept retroactively — identify one aspect of life in Australia that changed dramatically between 1800 and 1900 and one that showed remarkable continuity, and explain what drove each pattern
nodes.hinge_reason: The analytical framework is the prerequisite for the content nodes. Students who cannot hold continuity and change as coexisting analytical categories will produce accounts that only describe change, missing the significant continuities in living conditions, social structure and cultural life that the descriptor specifically requires.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat 'continuity and change' as simply 'what changed' — omitting continuities as though they are less historically interesting. Making both equally requiring explanation is the analytical scaffold for this descriptor.

success_criteria: Distinguishes continuity from change and explains why both require historical explanation
Applies the continuity-change framework to identify one continuity and one change in a given domain

nodes.label: Living and working conditions around 1900 — comparison across settings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe living and working conditions in Australia around 1900, compare different settings (rural vs urban, rich vs poor), and identify the main features of housing, sanitation, transport, education and industry.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least three domains of living/working conditions around 1900 (e.g. housing, sanitation, transport) and identify at least one significant difference between rural and urban settings or between social classes.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe conditions across all five domains named in the elaborations (housing, sanitation, transport, education, agriculture/industry); use primary sources such as photographs, paintings, diaries and newspapers to ground descriptions; compare rural and urban settings; compare wealthy and working-class experiences; describe the specific features of each domain — house types, water supply, horse-drawn vs early motor transport, school access, industrial vs agricultural work conditions.
wider: Use photographs and visual sources from around 1900 to compare living conditions — developing source analysis skills alongside content knowledge
Examine religious sectarianism (Protestant-Catholic tensions) and its social and political impacts — a less-examined dimension of Australian society at this time

response_modes.reason: Building an accurate picture of living conditions around 1900 across multiple domains requires encountering multiple types of evidence — photographs, diaries, official records — rather than relying on a single narrative account. The picture emerges from accumulation.

success_criteria: Describes living and working conditions in at least three domains around 1900
Identifies at least one significant difference between settings (e.g. rural/urban, rich/poor)

nodes.label: Change over time — comparing 1800 and 1900
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare living and working conditions around 1900 with those around 1800, identifying what changed, what persisted, and explaining what drove the changes.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two specific changes between 1800 and 1900 in living or working conditions and explain what drove each change.
nodes.typical_width: Students compare conditions systematically across domains — what was different in transport, housing, sanitation, education, and industry between early colonisation (1800) and the new federation (1900); explain what drove changes (industrialisation, population growth, improved technology, colonial wealth); identify persistent inequalities and conditions that changed little for First Nations Australians and the poorest workers; explain how the comparison illuminates the trajectory of development.
wider: Identify an aspect of life that showed strong continuity across the 1800–1900 period — examining what this persistence reveals about the limits of colonial development and who benefited from change and who did not
Compare the pace of change in different colonies — did all colonies develop at the same rate, and what explains the differences?

response_modes.reason: Students commonly identify changes between 1800 and 1900 without explaining the drivers — treating change as self-evident. Making the causal reasoning explicit (what drove the change, not just that it happened) is the core analytical demand of this node.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific changes in living or working conditions between 1800 and 1900
Explains what drove at least one of those changes

nodes.label: Legal reforms and their effects on living conditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how laws made by the new federal parliament — including the Harvester Judgment and the introduction of pensions — affected working conditions and standards of living.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the Harvester Judgment (establishing a minimum wage) and at least one other reform (e.g. aged pension), and explain the effect of each on working conditions or living standards.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the Harvester Judgment (1907) — its basis in a 'fair and reasonable' wage sufficient for a family, its legal mechanism, and its effects on wages and industrial relations; the introduction of old-age and invalid pensions; the arbitration system as a mechanism for resolving industrial disputes; explain how these legal changes represented a distinctly Australian approach to worker protection; connect to the labour movement context from K02 and the broader political context of the new Federal Parliament.
wider: Evaluate the limits of the Harvester Judgment — who was included and excluded from 'fair and reasonable' wage protection? Examine whether women and non-white workers benefited equally
Compare the Australian approach to labour reform with that of Britain and the USA in the same period — was Australia exceptional, and if so, why?

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe the Harvester Judgment as an unqualified achievement without examining who was excluded from its protections. Multiple examples of legal reforms — with their inclusions and exclusions — build a more accurate picture of the early federal legislative agenda.

success_criteria: Describes the Harvester Judgment and explains its effect on wages and working conditions
Describes at least one other federal legal reform and explains its effect on living standards
